analysis.one_liner: Expands the refundable child tax credit, helps disaster victims, boosts low-income housing tax credits, and restores business tax breaks.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 357-70 with strong bipartisan support, but the Senate fell short 48-44 on the procedural vote needed to even begin debating it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill was a bipartisan compromise on taxes. For families, it makes the refundable part of the child tax credit larger and counts each child, so bigger low-income families get more back on their taxes, and it lets people whose income dropped use last year's earnings for tax credits. It also makes payments to wildfire victims and East Palestine train derailment victims tax-free, expands the low-income housing tax credit, and restores business tax breaks for research spending and equipment purchases. The House passed it overwhelmingly, but Senate Republicans blocked the vote needed to start Senate debate, and the bill expired at the end of the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income families with children gain the most directly: the maximum refundable child tax credit rises to $1,800, $1,900, and $2,000 per child over 2023-2025, and the refundable amount is multiplied by the number of children, so larger families with modest earnings get bigger refunds. People who received compensation for wildfire losses or the East Palestine derailment would not pay tax on those payments. Developers building low-income rental housing get a larger tax credit. Businesses—especially those doing domestic research and buying equipment—gain from restored immediate expensing and bonus depreciation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Working families, disaster victims, and businesses

how_it_helps.text: Increases the maximum refundable child tax credit to $1,800 in 2023, $1,900 in 2024, and $2,000 in 2025, and applies the refundable amount per qualifying child, so larger families with low incomes receive more.
Lets taxpayers elect in 2024 and 2025 to use their prior year's earned income when calculating the child tax credit and earned income tax credit, cushioning families whose income fell.

Excludes from taxable income the compensation wildfire victims received for losses, and treats East Palestine train derailment payments from Norfolk Southern and governments as tax-free disaster relief.
Increases the low-income housing tax credit ceiling to 12.5% for 2023-2025 and lowers the bond-financing threshold to 30%, supporting construction of affordable rental housing.
Restores immediate deduction of domestic research costs through 2025, extends 100% bonus depreciation through 2026, and raises expensing limits for business assets to $1.29 million.
Sets special tax rules for Taiwanese residents and authorizes the President to negotiate a U.S.-Taiwan tax agreement to prevent double taxation.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost, since the CRS summaries list no offsetting tax increases, meaning the bill adds to deficits that taxpayers ultimately cover. A large share of the cost goes to business tax breaks whose benefits flow to companies and their owners. Raising the 1099 reporting threshold from $600 to $1,000 also means less income gets reported to the IRS, which slightly weakens enforcement.

drawbacks.text: The family and disaster provisions are temporary: the larger refundable credit amounts apply only to 2023-2025 and the disaster exclusions cover payments received through 2025.

The refundable child tax credit remains tied to earned income, so families with little or no earnings see little or none of the increase—the bill does not make the credit fully available to the poorest families.

Roughly half the bill's content is business tax relief—research expensing, bonus depreciation, and higher expensing limits—that primarily reduces taxes for profitable companies rather than helping households directly.
Raising the independent contractor reporting threshold from $600 to $1,000 means less income is reported to the IRS, reducing the information available for tax enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The family, disaster, and housing provisions deliver real, targeted help to low-income households, though the family help is temporary and still phases in with earnings. The business tax provisions are the bill's biggest cost driver and their benefits accrue mainly to companies; supporters argued restoring research expensing protects jobs and innovation, while critics noted the bill added to deficits with no pay-fors. The package was a genuine trade rather than one-sided, but the working-family benefits were the smaller and shorter-lived part of the deal.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 357-70, but when Senate Majority Leader Schumer brought it up in August 2024, Republicans blocked the 60-vote procedural step needed to start debate, the Senate never voted on the bill itself, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Ways and Means Committee reported the bill on a 40-3 vote within days of its introduction, an unusually fast bipartisan markup.
The House passed the bill under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure, which requires a two-thirds majority, by a vote of 357-70 on January 31, 2024, with 188 Democrats and 169 Republicans in favor.
The Senate received the bill on February 1, 2024, and it sat on the Senate calendar for nearly six months before a motion to proceed was made in late July 2024.

On August 1, 2024, cloture on the motion to proceed—a procedural vote requiring 60 senators just to begin considering the bill—failed 48-44, with 43 of 44 voting Democrats in favor and only 3 of 44 voting Republicans.
Because the motion to proceed failed, the Senate never debated or voted on the bill itself, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Senate Republicans who opposed the bill got the stall they sought, so no new business tax changes took effect and no deficit cost was added. Low-income families with children, disaster victims, and the businesses that would have gained from restored research expensing all lost the benefits they would have received.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Senate Republicans who stalled the bill

for.name: Rep. Jason Smith
for.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, negotiated the bipartisan compromise behind it, and managed its floor passage in the House.

for.name: House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Marked up and reported the bill 40-3 within two days of introduction.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the Senate floor in July 2024, filed the cloture motion, and moved to reconsider after the vote failed.

for.name: Senate Democrats and allied independents
for.what_they_did: Voted to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed so the Senate could take up the bill.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against cloture on the motion to proceed, denying the 60 votes needed to begin debate and keeping the bill off the Senate floor.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Led Republican opposition to taking up the bill in the Senate, arguing its design and cost were unacceptable.

against.name: House opponents
against.what_they_did: Voted against final passage in the House, though the bill still cleared the two-thirds threshold.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was strongly bipartisan—188 of 211 voting Democrats and 169 of 216 voting Republicans in favor—but Senate consideration split mostly by party: 45 of 48 votes to proceed came from Democrats and independents, while only 3 of 44 voting Republicans supported moving forward.
